outline.description: Identify the case name, court, judges, procedural posture, and disposition.
key_points: Court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit.
Case name: United States of America v. Edward Constantinescu; Perry “PJ” Matlock; John Rybarczyk; Gary Deel; Stefan Hrvatin; Tom Cooperman; Mitchell Hennessey; Daniel Knight.
Panel: Judges Higginson, Willett, and Engelhardt; opinion by Judge Engelhardt.
Appeal from: United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas (USDC Nos. 4:22-CR-612-1 through -8).
Procedural posture: Government (Plaintiff–Appellant) appealed the district court’s order dismissing a superseding indictment for failure to state an offense.
Disposition: Reversed and remanded.

outline.description: Summarize the key facts, the parties’ roles, the alleged conduct, charges, and any notable background relevant to the legal issues.
key_points: Defendants were social media personalities with large followings who held themselves out as skilled stock traders.

Alleged scheme: a pump-and-dump operation in which defendants would (1) purchase securities, (2) post false and misleading statements on social media to induce followers and other investors to buy and inflate prices, and (3) secretly sell (dump) their own holdings at the inflated prices.
Misrepresentations included their trading positions and price predictions/targets, which allegedly induced purchases and artificially inflated prices.
Alleged profits from the scheme totaled approximately $114 million.
Victims: followers and other investors who, relying on defendants’ posts, purchased the touted securities.
Charges: conspiracy to commit securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349); substantive securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1348) and aiding and abetting (18 U.S.C. § 2).

Procedural background: Defendant Knight pleaded guilty; remaining defendants moved to dismiss; the district court dismissed the indictment, holding it failed to allege deprivation of a traditional property interest (viewing the case as about withholding valuable economic information). The government appealed.

outline.description: State the specific legal questions the court addressed.
key_points: Whether the superseding indictment adequately alleged a “scheme to defraud” under 18 U.S.C. § 1348 by targeting a traditional property interest (money or property), as opposed to merely depriving victims of valuable economic information prohibited by Ciminelli’s rejection of the right-to-control theory.

Whether the indictment adequately alleged the requisite “intent to defraud,” even if defendants primarily intended to profit and victims may have received market-value securities, in light of the Supreme Court’s clarification in Kousisis regarding fraudulent-inducement fraud.

outline.description: Provide the court’s answers to each issue.
key_points: Yes. The indictment sufficiently alleged a scheme to defraud victims of money/property by fraudulently inducing them to purchase securities; it does not rest on a right-to-control theory barred by Ciminelli.

Yes. The indictment sufficiently alleged intent to defraud; under Kousisis, fraud does not require an intent to cause net economic harm or that victims suffer loss, so long as obtaining money or property is an object of the scheme.
Result: The district court’s dismissal is reversed; the case is remanded.

outline.description: Explain the court’s legal analysis, including how it applied statutes and precedents to the facts. Organize by the court’s analytical steps.
key_points: Elements and framework: Section 1348’s securities-fraud provision borrows key concepts from mail and wire fraud. The government must allege (1) a scheme to defraud and (2) an intent to defraud. A scheme to defraud entails a material misrepresentation intended to deceive to obtain something of value; intent to defraud entails intent to deceive and to cause some harm flowing from the deceit. The defendants conceded deception; they challenged the scheme-to-defraud and intent elements.

Scheme to defraud versus right-to-control: The district court viewed the indictment as alleging only deprivation of valuable economic information, invoking Ciminelli’s bar on the right-to-control theory. But the indictment here alleges fraudulent inducement: defendants used false statements to induce followers to buy securities, thereby parting with money. Fraudulent inducement protects traditional property interests (money/property) and is not a repackaged right-to-control theory.

Ciminelli distinguished: Ciminelli held that depriving a victim of valuable economic information alone is not fraud because the right to control assets is not a traditional property interest. Here, by contrast, the government alleged that victims were induced to transfer money to buy securities. Thus, the property interest targeted was money, placing the case outside Ciminelli’s prohibition.

Kousisis confirmation: The Supreme Court clarified that a fraudulent-inducement theory—using a material misstatement to trick a victim into a transaction that requires handing over money or property—remains valid and “protects money and property,” not merely information. Therefore, an indictment resting on fraudulent inducement does not run afoul of Ciminelli.

Intent to defraud and economic loss: Defendants argued they intended only to profit, not to harm anyone, and investors received market-value securities. Kousisis squarely rejects any requirement that the fraudster seek to cause net pecuniary loss or that the victim suffer such loss. A fraud is complete when the defendant induces the victim to part with money or property under materially false pretenses; providing something of equal value in return does not negate fraud liability.

Application to the indictment: The indictment alleges defendants posted false and misleading information “so that other investors were induced to purchase” the securities, and then secretly sold at a profit. Those allegations show the object was to obtain money from victims, satisfying intent to defraud under Kousisis. The profit motive evidences that defendants “had money in mind,” and the allegation of induced purchases sufficiently alleges injury for fraud purposes.

Supporting circuit precedent: The court cited Fifth Circuit authority (Greenlaw and Evans) for the § 1348 elements, and Baker for the proposition that fraud does not require a mirror-image victim loss matching the defendant’s gain. It also noted a Seventh Circuit decision applying Kousisis in a similar context.

Indictment sufficiency standard: On a motion to dismiss, courts take indictment allegations as true and ask whether each material element is alleged. Here, the indictment enumerated the elements and fairly informed defendants of the charges, thus satisfying Rule 7 requirements and protecting against double jeopardy.

outline.description: Extract the governing legal principles the court applied or clarified.
key_points: Indictment sufficiency: An indictment is sufficient if it (1) alleges each material element of the offense, (2) fairly informs the defendant of the charge, and (3) enables a double-jeopardy defense; on a motion to dismiss, courts take the allegations as true and review de novo.
Securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1348: Requires a scheme to defraud and an intent to defraud; courts may look to mail/wire fraud precedents to construe these elements.
Scheme to defraud: A material misrepresentation or omission intended to deceive another to obtain money or property.

Intent to defraud: Intent to deceive and to cause harm resulting from the deceit; after Kousisis, the required “harm” does not mean seeking net pecuniary loss—what matters is that obtaining money or property is an object of the scheme.
Ciminelli (right-to-control): The deprivation of valuable economic information alone is not a traditional property interest and cannot support fraud liability.

Fraudulent-inducement theory (Kousisis): Using a material misstatement to induce a victim to enter a transaction requiring the transfer of money or property states a valid fraud theory and is distinct from, and not barred by, the right-to-control theory.
Fraud completion: Fraud is complete when the victim is induced to part with money or property under materially false pretenses, even if the victim receives market-value goods or services in exchange.

outline.description: Note any separate opinions and their key arguments, or state if none.
key_points: No concurring or dissenting opinions; unanimous panel opinion authored by Judge Engelhardt.

outline.description: Explain the case’s doctrinal importance and practical implications.
key_points: Clarifies post-Ciminelli that securities-fraud indictments premised on fraudulent inducement to purchase securities—common in pump-and-dump and social-media influencer cases—target traditional property (money) and are legally sufficient.
Confirms that § 1348’s elements are analyzed in tandem with mail/wire fraud jurisprudence and that the fraudulent-inducement theory remains a viable framework for federal fraud prosecutions.
Emphasizes that neither actual economic loss nor an intent to cause such loss is required; the government need only show that obtaining money or property was an object of the deceptive scheme.

Guides district courts on motions to dismiss indictments post-Ciminelli and Kousisis: courts must distinguish between right-to-control theories and traditional property-based fraudulent inducement and must accept well-pleaded allegations as true.
Signals robust applicability of federal fraud statutes to contemporary market manipulation conducted via social media.
